intro: MITRE ATT&CK is the shared language defenders use to describe adversary behavior. This module teaches how the Enterprise matrix is organized, how to map incidents and detection rules to technique IDs, how to find and prioritize coverage gaps against realistic threat actors, and how to build and share ATT&CK Navigator layers. These skills turn raw alerts and reports into structured evidence that guides detection engineering, hunting and executive reporting.

lessons.title: ATT&CK matrix structure
lessons.why: Every modern SOC speaks ATT&CK. Knowing how the matrix is organized lets you read threat reports, rules and incident notes without guessing.

p: MITRE ATT&CK is a publicly maintained knowledge base of adversary behavior built from real-world observations. It is not a checklist, a product or a scoring standard. It describes what attackers do after and during an intrusion so defenders can describe, detect and compare behavior using shared vocabulary. There are separate matrices for Enterprise (Windows, macOS, Linux, cloud, containers, network), Mobile and ICS. This module focuses on Enterprise. The content is versioned, so technique names and counts change between releases; always record which version your team maps against, and do not memorize totals, memorize the structure.

Tactics are the columns of the matrix and represent the adversary's short-term goal at a stage of an operation. In the traditional Enterprise ordering they are: Reconnaissance (TA0043), Resource Development (TA0042), Initial Access (TA0001), Execution (TA0002), Persistence (TA0003), Privilege Escalation (TA0004), Defense Evasion (TA0005), Credential Access (TA0006), Discovery (TA0007), Lateral Movement (TA0008), Collection (TA0009), Command and Control (TA0011), Exfiltration (TA0010) and Impact (TA0040). That is 14 tactics. The order is a logical flow, not a strict sequence; attackers loop, skip and repeat tactics. Newer releases may reorganize tactics, so check the current matrix.

A technique is how a goal is achieved, identified by a T-number such as T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter. A sub-technique adds a dot and three digits for a more specific method: T1059.001 is PowerShell, T1059.003 is Windows Command Shell. A technique can appear under more than one tactic, for example Valid Accounts (T1078) supports Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation and Defense Evasion. The tactic is the column, the technique is the cell; to reference a cell unambiguously you may write the tactic and ID together.

Each technique page lists a description, procedure examples (named groups and software that used it), mitigations (M-numbers such as M1017 User Training), detection guidance and data sources with data components such as Process Creation or Network Traffic Content. Defenders mostly use three parts: procedure examples to learn how real actors implement it, data sources to learn which logs you need, and mitigations to plan prevention. Groups carry G-numbers (G0016 style) and software carries S-numbers. Treat detection text as a starting idea, not a finished rule.

Practice by taking one public threat report and listing every behavior it describes, then looking up each in the matrix. Beginners often find that a single paragraph of a report yields three or four techniques. Over time you will recognize the common ones by sight: PowerShell, scheduled tasks, Run keys, RDP, credential dumping and shadow copy deletion appear in a large share of intrusions. Keep a personal cheat sheet of the twenty IDs you meet most often and update it as you learn.

lessons.title: Mapping incidents to techniques
lessons.why: Mapping turns a messy narrative into structured, comparable evidence that supports reporting, hunting and trend analysis.

p: Mapping begins with what the adversary did, expressed as an action on a system, not the name of a malware family or a vague label like 'hacking'. Write each observation as a short sentence: 'user opened a .docm attachment', 'winword.exe spawned powershell.exe with an encoded command', 'rundll32 accessed lsass memory'. Then find the technique whose description matches the action. Avoid mapping from tool names alone, because tools can implement many techniques and the same technique can be reached with many tools. Evidence should be attached to every mapping so a reviewer can verify it.

Common mappings include: phishing email with a malicious attachment, T1566.001; user double-clicking the attachment, T1204.002 User Execution: Malicious File; PowerShell running an encoded command, T1059.001 plus T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information; dumping LSASS memory, T1003.001; creating a scheduled task for persistence, T1053.005; a Run key value in the registry, T1547.001; remote desktop to another host, T1021.001; archiving files before transfer, T1560; upload to a cloud storage site, T1567; encrypting files, T1486; deleting shadow copies, T1490.

Prefer the sub-technique when evidence supports it, and the parent technique when it does not. If you only know a command shell was used but not which, map T1059. Map one event to several techniques when it genuinely shows several behaviors, but do not inflate: one log line rarely proves five techniques. Record confidence (confirmed, likely, possible) and the evidence source such as an EDR event ID or a packet capture. A mapping without evidence is an opinion and degrades downstream trend data.

Place mapped techniques on a timeline and group them by tactic. The result is a story: Initial Access (T1566.001), Execution (T1204.002, T1059.001), Credential Access (T1003.001), Lateral Movement (T1021.001), Collection (T1560), Exfiltration (T1567), Impact (T1486). Gaps in the story are valuable: if you see lateral movement but no credential access, either logging missed it or the adversary reused known credentials (T1078). Gaps become hunting leads and logging requests.

Be careful with ambiguity. A single behavior such as 'a service was installed' can be persistence (T1543.003), privilege escalation or lateral movement via service execution (T1569.002), depending on context. When the same evidence fits more than one technique, state the competing options and the question that would settle it, for instance whether the service was created locally or remotely. Peer review of mappings is a cheap quality control: a second analyst maps the same notes independently and the team discusses differences.

lessons.title: Mapping detections to techniques
lessons.why: Tagging rules with technique IDs shows what you can detect, but only if the tag reflects real, working telemetry.

p: Each detection rule in a SIEM or EDR should carry one or more ATT&CK technique IDs in its metadata. Many rule formats support this directly; Sigma rules use a tags list such as attack.execution and attack.t1059.001. Tags let you filter rules by technique, report coverage, and link alerts to the matrix during triage. Tag the technique the rule is designed to catch, not every technique that could ever produce a similar log. Over-tagging makes coverage look better than it is and misleads leadership.

A rule only works if its data source is collected. A rule for T1003.001 that depends on process access events to lsass.exe (Sysmon event ID 10) is worthless where that event is not logged. For each rule record the required data source and component, the log source, the parsing field names, and whether collection is verified. A coverage claim has three conditions: the rule exists, the data flows, and the rule has been tested. Missing any one means the technique is not truly covered.

Not all detections of a technique are equal. A rule matching the single string 'mimikatz' catches one tool and is trivial to evade; a rule on suspicious access rights to LSASS from unusual processes catches the behavior. Rate rules by robustness (behavior versus indicator), false positive rate, and the procedures they cover. A technique has many procedures, so one rule usually covers only a slice. Many teams score coverage as none, partial or good, and require a test, such as an atomic simulation, to move up a level.

Review tags when rules change. Retire tags for rules that were disabled or tuned so heavily they no longer fire. Record the date of the last successful test. When an alert fires, record the technique so you can later measure how often each technique truly produces confirmed incidents versus noise. This feedback turns the matrix from a poster into a measurement system for the detection program.

Share the ATT&CK tags with other teams. Threat intelligence analysts tag reports, detection engineers tag rules, and incident responders tag cases. When all three use the same IDs, you can query across them: which techniques did our last five incidents use, which of those have tested rules, and which actors in our intelligence feed use them. That single question is the entire value of the framework in practice, and it only works when tags are consistent and honest.

snippet.label: Sigma-style tags
snippet.text:
title: Encoded PowerShell Command
status: test
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1027

lessons.example: A team claims coverage of T1003.001 because a rule exists. The reviewer checks: the rule needs Sysmon event ID 10, but only half the servers run Sysmon, and the rule was last tested a year ago. Coverage is rated partial: tagged, partly collected, untested. The action items are to deploy Sysmon to the remaining servers and run a safe simulation to confirm the alert fires.

lessons.title: Coverage and gap analysis
lessons.why: You cannot cover every technique. Gap analysis helps you spend limited engineering time on the behaviors that most threaten your organization.

p: Coverage analysis begins with a threat model, not the whole matrix. Pick the threat actors and malware that realistically target your sector, using intelligence reports and the Groups and Software pages of ATT&CK. Extract their technique lists. Then compare those lists to your tagged detections. The overlap is covered; the rest are gaps. A retailer, a hospital and a bank face different actors, so their priority lists differ, and a generic 'cover everything' goal wastes effort on techniques nobody in your threat set uses.

For each gap technique weigh four factors: how many relevant actors use it, how much damage it enables, whether the required data is already collected, and how reliably a detection can be written. Techniques used by many actors and by ransomware affiliates, such as T1059.001, T1003.001, T1021.001 and T1486, usually rank high. Techniques with high prevalence but no data source rank as logging projects first. Techniques with noisy, benign-looking activity, such as T1082 System Information Discovery, may rank low because a rule would drown analysts.

sections.h: Detection is not the only control
p: A gap does not always require a new alert. Check mitigations: Attack Surface Reduction rules, application control, disabling macros from the internet, MFA and network segmentation may prevent the technique entirely. Prevention plus a lightweight detection can beat a complex rule. Also record where you rely on a single control; if one rule is your only view of T1021.001, a bypass leaves you blind. Layered coverage per critical technique is a better target than one-rule coverage of many techniques.

Present results as a short prioritized list with owner and due date, not a rainbow heatmap alone. Revisit after each quarter or after a major intelligence change. Track metrics such as percent of top-twenty actor techniques with tested detections, mean time to implement a new detection, and confirmed true positives per technique. Avoid vanity metrics like total technique count tagged, which rewards over-tagging rather than protection.

A final caution: ATT&CK describes known behavior, so a complete green map does not mean you are safe. Adversaries invent new procedures, and some activities are not captured as techniques at all. Use the matrix to organize what you know and to expose blind spots, then supplement it with threat hunting, red team exercises and incident lessons learned. Treat coverage as a living estimate that is refreshed whenever the environment, the actors or the matrix version change.

lessons.example: A regional hospital identifies three ransomware affiliates as its main threat. Their shared techniques include T1003.001, T1021.001 and T1490. Detections exist for none with tests. Data for T1021.001 is already collected from Windows logon events (4624, logon type 10), so that rule is quick; T1003.001 needs Sysmon rollout first. The team schedules T1021.001 this month and the Sysmon rollout next.

lessons.title: ATT&CK Navigator and layers
lessons.why: Navigator turns your analysis into a shareable visual, and layers keep the underlying data portable and versioned.

p: ATT&CK Navigator is a free, open-source web tool that displays the matrix and lets you annotate it. You can run it from the public MITRE-hosted page or host your own copy so no data leaves your network, which matters for sensitive coverage information. Everything you annotate is saved as a layer, a JSON file you can download, share and reopen. Layers are independent of the ATT&CK content version, but each layer records the version and Navigator version it was built for, so older layers remain readable.

Each technique cell can carry a score (numeric, often 0 to 100), a color, a comment and metadata. A common scheme gives detection coverage a score from 0 to 3 or 0 to 100 and a gradient color from red to green. Comments hold the rule names, data sources and test dates. You can filter by platform, such as Windows, and hide sub-techniques you do not track. Keep a legend in the layer description so viewers know what colors mean; a heatmap without a legend invites misreading.

Create separate layers for each question: one for the threat actor technique list (score 1 for used), one for your detections (score 1 for covered), and one for prevention. Use the layer-combination expression, such as a+b, to merge scores; with actor score 1 and detection score 1, a cell scoring 1 is an uncovered threat technique. Some teams assign the actor layer 2 and detection layer 1 so that results of 2 equal gaps, 3 equal covered threats and 1 equals coverage without a known threat need. Document the expression with the layer.

Export as JSON for storage in version control, and as SVG or Excel for reports. The JSON stores a list of techniques with fields techniqueID, tactic, score, color and comment. Version control gives you history of how coverage changed. In presentations, show one clear message per slide, such as the top five gaps, rather than the whole matrix. Pair the image with the prioritized action list from your gap analysis so leadership sees decisions, not decoration.

Keep the layer files small, named consistently and dated, such as detections-2026-Q3.json. Store them next to the rule repository so that a rule change and the coverage change appear in the same review. Some teams generate the detection layer automatically from rule tags with a script, which removes manual drift. Whatever you do, avoid hand-colored heatmaps that nobody can reproduce; a layer that cannot be regenerated or explained will be distrusted the first time someone challenges it.

lessons.example: The analyst builds layer A with scores of 1 for every technique used by an actor group, and layer B with scores of 1 for tested detections. Combining with a+b shows cells at 2 for covered threat techniques and cells at 1 for either an untested gap or an unneeded detection. She filters to score 1 from layer A only, exports a list of five uncovered techniques, and attaches the SVG and the JSON to her quarterly review.

labs.title: Map the intrusion
labs.scenario: You receive notes from a fictional incident at example.com. A phishing email delivered invoice.docm to a user on host WS-14 (192.0.2.44). The macro launched PowerShell, a credential dump followed, the attacker used RDP to reach FS-02 (192.0.2.60), zipped documents and uploaded them to a file-sharing site, then encrypted shares. The goal is a clean diagram a reviewer could audit event by event, with each placement justified by an observed action rather than assumption.
labs.objective: Place each observed event on the correct tactic column with the right technique ID.

steps.do: Drag 'phishing email with invoice.docm' to a column
steps.see: Placed under Initial Access. Suggested ID: T1566.001

steps.do: Drag 'user opened attachment, macro ran PowerShell encoded command'
steps.see: Placed under Execution. IDs: T1204.002, T1059.001

steps.do: Drag 'lsass.exe memory read by rundll32'
steps.see: Placed under Credential Access. ID: T1003.001

steps.do: Drag 'RDP logon to FS-02'
steps.see: Placed under Lateral Movement. ID: T1021.001

steps.do: Drag 'documents.zip created on FS-02'
steps.see: Placed under Collection. ID: T1560

steps.do: Drag 'upload to file-sharing site' and 'shares encrypted'
steps.see: Exfiltration T1567; Impact T1486. Diagram complete: 7 tactics linked in time order.

labs.answer: The chain is Initial Access T1566.001, Execution T1204.002 and T1059.001, Credential Access T1003.001, Lateral Movement T1021.001, Collection T1560, Exfiltration T1567 and Impact T1486, ordered by timestamp. Note the gaps in the story, such as the unknown initial access timing, and list them as follow-up questions.
labs.hint: Ask what the attacker was trying to achieve at each step; that is the tactic.

labs.title: Tag the rules
labs.scenario: Your fictional SIEM holds ten detection rules with no ATT&CK tags. Management wants a coverage report by Friday. You must assign each rule a technique ID and write the data source it needs, without over-tagging. Management expects the report to be defensible, so each tag must come with a short note about the log field the rule uses.
labs.objective: Tag ten rules with technique IDs and required data sources.

steps.do: Open rule 'Encoded PowerShell command line'
steps.see: Query on process_creation CommandLine contains -enc. Tag T1059.001. Needs: Process Creation with command line.

steps.do: Open rule 'Scheduled task created via schtasks'
steps.see: Event ID 4698 or Sysmon 1. Tag T1053.005.

steps.do: Open rule 'New Run key value'
steps.see: Sysmon event 13. Tag T1547.001. Needs: Registry Key Modification.

steps.do: Open rule 'LSASS access with 0x1010 rights'
steps.see: Sysmon event 10. Tag T1003.001. Needs: Process Access.

steps.do: Open rule 'vssadmin delete shadows'
steps.see: Process creation. Tag T1490.

steps.do: Open rule 'Logon type 10 from new source'
steps.see: Event 4624. Tag T1021.001. Needs: Logon Session Creation.

steps.do: Open rule 'Security log cleared (1102)'
steps.see: Tag T1070.001. Needs: Windows event log.

steps.do: Save all ten and view report
steps.see: Report: 10 rules tagged, 3 rules flagged 'data source not collected on 40 percent of hosts'.

labs.answer: Tags: T1059.001, T1053.005, T1547.001, T1003.001, T1490, T1021.001, T1070.001 and the remaining rules by their behavior, each with the matching data source. Flag rules whose data source is not collected everywhere as partial coverage. Also record the test date for each rule so that partial or untested coverage is distinguishable from verified coverage.
labs.hint: Match the log field the rule uses to the data component, then to the technique.

labs.title: Build a Navigator layer
labs.scenario: A fictional ransomware group, 'Group-X', is your top threat. You have its technique list and your list of tested detections. Build layers and read the gap view to decide where to focus next. Treat the numbers as a planning aid; the point is to read which cells are threats without detections and decide what to do about them.
labs.objective: Combine actor and detection scores and read the uncovered techniques.

steps.do: Create layer 'Actor' and score 1 for T1566.001, T1059.001, T1003.001, T1021.001, T1490, T1486
steps.see: Layer saved: 6 techniques scored 1.

steps.do: Create layer 'Detections' and score 1 for T1059.001, T1486
steps.see: Layer saved: 2 techniques scored 1.

steps.do: Set an expression a+b into a third layer
steps.see: Combined layer: T1059.001=2, T1486=2, others=1.

steps.do: Set a comment legend: 2 covered threat, 1 gap
steps.see: Legend stored in layer description.

steps.do: Filter to score 1 and view the list
Export JSON
steps.see: File gap-view.json exported (6 techniques).

labs.answer: Covered threat techniques are T1059.001 and T1486. Gaps are T1566.001, T1003.001, T1021.001 and T1490, which become the prioritized list pending data availability. The combined view lets you hand management a short ordered list instead of an unreadable heatmap.
labs.hint: Cells that only the actor layer marks are the gaps; the sum shows overlap.

labs.title: Choose the next detection
labs.scenario: Your lead asks which one uncovered technique you will build next. Options: T1003.001 (needs Sysmon, 50 percent hosts), T1021.001 (Windows logon events already collected), T1082 (noisy). Group-X uses all three. Your lead values reasoning more than the final pick, so explain the trade-offs aloud before committing to one technique.
labs.objective: Justify one choice based on actor use and available logs.

steps.do: Ask lead: how many actors use each?
steps.see: Lead: 'T1003.001 and T1021.001 are used by every affiliate; T1082 by all but it is very noisy.'

steps.do: Ask: which logs do we already collect?
steps.see: Lead: 'Event 4624 with logon type is in the SIEM; Sysmon is on half the servers.'

steps.do: Propose T1021.001 first
steps.see: Lead: 'Why not LSASS?'

steps.do: Explain: data exists now and the rule is feasible with low noise
steps.see: Lead: 'Good. And LSASS?'

steps.do: Propose a Sysmon rollout ticket for T1003.001
steps.see: Lead: 'Approved. Write the rule, test it, then tag it.'

steps.do: Submit your plan
steps.see: Plan accepted: T1021.001 rule this sprint, Sysmon rollout next, T1082 deferred.

labs.answer: Build T1021.001 first because it is widely used by relevant actors, the required logon data is already collected and it is feasible with modest noise. Open a logging project for T1003.001 and defer noisy T1082. Document why the others were deferred so the decision can be revisited when data or threats change.
labs.hint: Weigh actor use, data availability and noise together.
